description: Flame tests for metal ions, tests for gases, precipitate tests and instrumental analysis.
content_html:
Why We Need Chemical Tests

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances — whether to check the safety of a water supply, verify the purity of a product, identify minerals in rocks, or analyse a sample in a forensic investigation. Chemical identification tests — collectively known as qualitative analysis — fall into two broad categories: traditional wet chemistry tests that rely on observable changes, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more precise results.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Electrons in the metal ion absorb energy from the flame, are promoted to a higher energy level, and then release that energy as visible light at a characteristic wavelength. To carry out a flame test: clean a nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove residues from previous tests), dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The loop must be cleaned between each test to avoid contamination that could give a misleading result.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green or blue-green. Barium — apple-green.

Tests for Gases

You must be able to test for four common gases. Each test gives a distinctive, reproducible result:

  • Hydrogen — hold a lit splint near the mouth of the tube; a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen (it ignites and reacts with oxygen in the air).
  • Oxygen — insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion.
  • Carbon dioxide — bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); it turns milky (white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms): \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\).
  • Chlorine — hold damp litmus paper near the gas; it is first turned red (chlorine is acidic) then bleached white (chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent).

Testing for Metal Ions with Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to a solution containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The metal ions react with hydroxide ions to form insoluble metal hydroxides, whose colour identifies the ion present.

Calcium (Ca²♠): white precipitate. Copper(II) (Cu²♠): blue precipitate. Iron(II) (Fe²♠): green precipitate (\(Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\)). Iron(III) (Fe³♠): brown precipitate (\(Fe^{3+} + 3OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\)). Aluminium (Al³♠): white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric). Magnesium (Mg²♠): white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This distinction between aluminium and magnesium — both give white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves — is frequently tested.

Testing for Negative Ions (Anions)

Carbonate ions (CO&sub3;²♠): add dilute hydrochloric acid; if carbonates are present, carbon dioxide is produced (test it by bubbling through limewater — it turns milky). Sulfate ions (SO&sub4;²♠): acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid first (to remove interfering ions), then add barium chloride solution; a white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfates. Halide ions: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions give a white precipitate of silver chloride; bromide ions give a cream precipitate; iodide ions give a yellow precipitate.

Key Fact

Halide identification: add silver nitrate (after acidifying with dilute nitric acid). Chloride → white precipitate. Bromide → cream precipitate. Iodide → yellow precipitate. Always acidify first to remove carbonate or other interfering ions.

Systematic Approach to Identifying an Unknown Ionic Compound

When identifying an unknown ionic compound, work through the tests in a logical order. Begin by dissolving a small amount of the sample in distilled water. Carry out a flame test to identify the metal cation: note the colour carefully and compare against the reference list. If the flame test result is ambiguous (for example, a sodium impurity masking potassium), confirm using a sodium hydroxide precipitate test. Next, test for the anion: use dilute acid and limewater for carbonates, barium chloride solution for sulfates, and acidified silver nitrate for halides. Record all observations clearly — both positive (what you see) and negative (what is absent). Always repeat tests if an observation is unclear, and clean equipment between each test to avoid contamination.

Instrumental Methods and Flame Emission Spectroscopy (Higher Tier)

Instrumental methods such as gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (often combined as GC-MS) are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional wet chemistry tests. They can detect very small quantities of a substance and give quantitative results rather than just qualitative observations.

Flame emission spectroscopy passes the light from a flame test through a prism or diffraction grating to produce a spectrum of the light emitted by each element. Each element produces a unique set of coloured lines at specific wavelengths. Unlike a visual flame test, this technique can: detect very small quantities of metal ions, identify ions even when a mixture of metals is present (the spectrum shows lines for each), and give quantitative information about concentration (by measuring line intensity). A simple flame test only gives a single colour that may mask one ion when another is present (e.g. sodium’s intense yellow can mask potassium’s lilac).
exam_tip_html: For flame test and precipitate questions, you must state both the reagent used and the observation. Writing ‘add NaOH’ without stating the colour of the precipitate will not score the second mark. For gas tests, name both the test substance and the result (e.g. ‘glowing splint relights’ for oxygen — do not just write ‘splint test’). A common error is confusing the aluminium and magnesium precipitate tests — remember only aluminium’s white precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH. Higher Tier: in questions comparing flame tests with flame emission spectroscopy, focus on the advantages of the instrumental method: can detect mixtures, gives quantitative data, much higher sensitivity.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame test colours: lithium = crimson, sodium = yellow, potassium = lilac, calcium = orange-red, copper = green, barium = apple-green. Gas tests: hydrogen = squeaky pop; oxygen = relights glowing splint; CO&sub2; = turns limewater milky; chlorine = bleaches damp litmus paper.
  • NaOH precipitate tests: copper = blue; iron(II) = green; iron(III) = brown; calcium/magnesium = white (magnesium does not dissolve in excess; aluminium does). Halide ions tested with silver nitrate: chloride = white, bromide = cream, iodide = yellow (acidify first with dilute nitric acid).
  • Higher: Flame emission spectroscopy can identify mixtures of metal ions and gives quantitative data — advantages over a simple flame test. Instrumental methods (GC-MS) offer greater sensitivity, accuracy and speed than traditional wet chemistry tests.

practice_questions.text:
Which flame test colour is produced by sodium ions?
A) Crimson
B) Lilac
C) Yellow
D) Green
State the test used to identify carbon dioxide gas and the observation that confirms its presence.
practice_questions.marks: Bubble through limewater; it turns milky / cloudy (white precipitate forms). [1 mark — both test and observation required]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would test an unknown solution to determine whether it contains iron(II) or iron(III) ions.
practice_questions.marks: Add sodium hydroxide solution to the unknown solution [1 mark]; iron(II) ions give a green precipitate; iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate [1 mark — must distinguish between the two colours].

practice_questions.text: A student adds silver nitrate solution to two unknown solutions and observes a cream precipitate in one and a yellow precipitate in the other. Explain what ions are present in each solution and why the student must acidify the solutions before adding silver nitrate.
practice_questions.marks: Cream precipitate = bromide ions (Br⁻) [1 mark]; yellow precipitate = iodide ions (I⁻) [1 mark]; acidifying (with dilute nitric acid) removes carbonate ions or other ions that would form precipitates with silver nitrate and give misleading results [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
An unknown ionic compound is dissolved in water. A flame test produces an orange-red colour. Adding sodium hydroxide solution produces a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

(a) Identify the metal ion present. [1 mark]
(b) Explain how you would determine whether a sulfate ion is present in the solution. [3 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Calcium (Ca²⁺) — orange-red flame, white precipitate with NaOH that does not dissolve [1 mark]; (b) Add dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions that might interfere [1 mark]; add barium chloride solution [1 mark]; a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO₄) confirms sulfate ions are present [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Describe how instrumental methods of analysis, such as flame emission spectroscopy, differ from traditional chemical tests such as the flame test. Include the advantages of instrumental methods and explain when a traditional flame test might give a misleading result.

Higher Tier candidates should include detail on how flame emission spectroscopy works.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation that flame emission spectroscopy separates light from the flame into a spectrum of characteristic wavelength lines unique to each element; can identify mixtures because each element contributes its own spectral lines (unlike a single-colour flame test which can be masked by sodium yellow); gives quantitative information from line intensity; much higher sensitivity for detecting trace amounts. Traditional flame test limitations clearly stated: cannot distinguish mixtures, qualitative only, relies on human colour perception. Specific example of sodium masking potassium in a flame test.
Secure: Two or more advantages of instrumental methods correctly stated; limitation of flame test noted; how emission spectroscopy produces a spectrum described.
Developing: One advantage identified; some mention of spectrum or sensitivity; flame test limitation noted.
Emerging: Basic comparison made; limited detail on how either method works.

flashcard_questions.q: What colour does lithium produce in a flame test?
What colour does sodium produce in a flame test?
What colour does potassium produce in a flame test?
What colour does copper produce in a flame test?
What colour does calcium produce in a flame test?
What colour does barium produce in a flame test?
What is the test for oxygen gas?
flashcard_questions.a: A glowing splint relights in the gas.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the test for hydrogen gas?
flashcard_questions.a: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop.

flashcard_questions.q: What colour precipitate does iron(III) give with NaOH solution?
What colour precipitate does iron(II) give with NaOH solution?
How do you distinguish aluminium from magnesium using NaOH?
flashcard_questions.a: Both give a white precipitate, but aluminium's dissolves in excess NaOH; magnesium's does not.

flashcard_questions.q: What reagent is used to test for sulfate ions, and what is the positive result?
flashcard_questions.a: Barium chloride solution; a white precipitate of barium sulfate forms.

flashcard_questions.q: What colour precipitate does a chloride ion give with silver nitrate?

glossary_terms.definition: Tests carried out using chemical reagents that produce visible changes such as colour changes, precipitates or gas production.
Techniques that use machines such as spectrometers to identify substances quickly, accurately and with high sensitivity.
A test in which a sample is held in a Bunsen flame on a nichrome wire loop to identify metal ions by the characteristic colour produced.
Insoluble solids formed when two solutions are mixed and ions combine to form an insoluble compound.
BaCl₂ solution, used to test for sulfate ions; a white precipitate of barium sulfate is produced if sulfates are present.
Chemical analysis that identifies what substances are present in a sample, without measuring exact quantities.
